title: The Balloon and the Duck Pond
markdown:
The launch field lay like a map of weather, all wind-flags and rope, and at its heart stood Leonie March, who spoke silk as other people spoke English. Grease lived in the creases of her palms. She knew every seam of the emerald envelope by touch, every valve by the particular sigh it made when the air inside grew restless. Lift and pressure interested her more than applause. The Daily Chronicle’s crest shone on the balloon’s taut skin, a green leviathan impatient for the county.

Colonel Brass arrived as if the field had been invented for his waistcoat. Pomade defied gravity. Ambition did the same. “Patriotism in the Puff!” he declared, striking a pose that would have embarrassed marble. Cameras clustered. Scribes sharpened pencils. The flight was to cleave the heavens, traverse the entire county, and print itself into history before tea.

“Leonie, my dear,” Brass boomed, a trumpet with opinions. “The sky awaits its champion. Today we etch our names in the eternal scroll of daring!”

Leonie’s gaze had already left him. Near the inflation valve, a joint looked wrong: a gossamer fracture no larger than a ladybug’s sigh, a smell of strained rubber and coming weather. Her lens hovered. “Colonel. This valve is fragile. The forecast speaks of a rogue zephyr. The joint will not hold.”

Brass waved a hand and nearly felled a stack of flyers. “Fragile? Nonsense. It is built for glory, not dithering. The Chronicle expects fireworks, not meteorological minutiae. We are on the printing press’s schedule.” He winked at a scribe. The scribe, professionally, wrote down the wink.

Leonie did not argue. Argument was a kind of lift Brass understood. Needle and whisper-thin silk she understood better. While he arranged himself as a marble emperor for a swift sketch, her fingers patched the micro-tear, a quiet refusal of his timetable and a quiet acceptance of the sky’s. The crowd’s heat pressed her neck. Tar and grass. The valve still felt thin under her thumb.

Trumpets tore the air. The crowd erupted. Brass’s monocle performed a wild pirouette as he clambered into the wicker with theatrical flair. “To glory, my brave aeronauts!” Flashes popped like champagne corks. Leonie scrambled in with her toolkit, heart a drum solo she declined to conduct in public.

The balloon lurched skyward, a bruised-purple jewel against the fading light. For a breath the county unrolled beneath them, hedges and lanes and the small proud roofs of people who would buy tomorrow’s paper. Then the valve, despite the patch, began an apologetic hiss. Upward momentum faltered. Reversed.

“Faster, pilot, faster!” Brass boomed, mistaking descent for a calculated dive. “Demonstrate British engineering and unwavering nerve!” He was already composing the headline, tasting ink.

Leonie felt the drop in her knees, the unnerving tilt in her inner ear, the green coming up too fast. Below, not adoring crowds, but Mayor Grimshaw’s pumpkin patch: colossal gourds, each a cottage of orange pride, plump and perfect and catastrophically in the way. The balloon listed like a drunken galleon. Grimshaw emerged from his farmhouse, spectacles askew, horror assembling itself on a face already practised at scowling.

“My pumpkins!” he shrieked, a sound that could curdle milk.

Brass, ever the showman, rehearsed aloud: “A calculated, daring landing to showcase the resilience of the human spirit—”

Leonie took the rope. A directional vent. A tug that was not glory and not panic, only the language of air she had spent years learning. The envelope answered, sullenly. They missed the gourds. They did not miss the water. The balloon landed with a resounding sploosh in Mayor Grimshaw’s prize-winning, exceptionally muddy duck pond.

Ducks departed in a fury of opinion. Mud arrived in a fury of fact. Brass emerged a sodden silhouette, waistcoat a drowned relic, still attempting a heroic pose. “A watery triumph. A bold new paradigm in aeronautical arrival.” Water streamed from his chin. His hair, at last, obeyed gravity.

The cost of the save was visible: the Chronicle’s leviathan sagging in brown water, the patch she had sewn now a wet flag, Brass still talking. Leonie sat on the basket’s rim, toolkit open, and checked the valve as she would have checked it on the field, mud and all. The pond smelled of duck and crushed grass. Grimshaw’s pumpkins remained, smugly uncrushed.

The next morning the Daily Chronicle, to Brass’s sputtering disbelief, did not trumpet his bedraggled visage. The headline, colossal, proclaimed: MECHANIC’S MASTERFUL MANEUVER SAVES COUNTY’S CROPS. Beneath it, a sketch of Leonie, face smudged with mud and grease, eyes alight with the quiet satisfaction of a job done. She looked like a craftsman admiring her work, which is what she was.

Back on the launch field, the silk lay in drying folds. Leonie ran a thumb along a new seam. The wind, indifferent to headlines, offered a zephyr. She listened to it, as she always had, and reached for needle and patch before anyone asked her to pose.
characters: Leonie March (balloon mechanic), Colonel Brass (publicity addict)
